analysis.one_liner: Bans automated unsolicited text messages to cell phones without the recipient's prior consent.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2022 and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill expands the existing federal ban on unwanted automated calls — the telemarketing robocall rules — to cover automated text messages. Under it, a company could not use software to blast texts to your phone without your prior express consent, except for emergencies. It also directs the Federal Communications Commission to write rules defining key terms and creates a database so callers can check whether a phone number has been reassigned to a new owner.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who owns a cell phone. Unwanted automated texts are a growing nuisance — scam texts, spam promotions, and political blasts — and this bill would put them under the same consent rules that already apply to automated calls. Phone owners would gain a legal basis to stop or sue over unsolicited automated texts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the Communications Act's ban on automatic telephone dialing systems so it explicitly covers sending text messages, not just making calls, to numbers without the recipient's prior express consent [S3].

It removes the exception that allowed calls made to collect a debt owed to or guaranteed by the United States without consent, meaning even federal debt collectors would need consent to autodial or robotext a consumer [S3].

It requires the FCC, within 18 months of enactment, to issue a rule defining 'automatically,' 'dial,' 'send,' and 'charged for the call,' closing loopholes created by evolving dialing technology [S3].

It creates an FCC-maintained reassigned number database and a safe harbor so callers who check the database are not liable for texting a number that changed hands — reducing accidental wrong-number texts while keeping consent as the rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Text-message marketing companies, telemarketers, and collection agencies would lose a cheap channel for reaching consumers, since blasting automated texts without prior consent would become illegal. Businesses would bear the cost of checking consent and the reassigned-number database before texting.

drawbacks.text: The bill's safe harbor for reassigned numbers gives callers a way to avoid liability for wrong-number texts if they check the FCC database — a protection for businesses that consumer groups might view as diluting the consent rule, particularly if the database is incomplete [S3].

Removing the federal debt collection exception [S3] means agencies trying to reach borrowers about federal loans could no longer autodial them without consent, which could make it harder to reach some borrowers about delinquent debts.

The FCC rulemaking requires weighing 'modern dialing practices and consumer preferences' [S3], so the final definitions could end up narrower than the statutory language and undercut the ban's practical reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary phone owners, the benefit is straightforward: fewer unwanted automated texts and a clearer legal right to say no. The costs fall mainly on marketers and collectors, who would need consent and database checks — real but modest compliance burdens. The main design risk is that the FCC's definitions and the reassigned-number safe harbor could soften the ban in practice, but the bill's core consent requirement is a clear gain for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2022 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on July 12, 2022, with six Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Porter, Norton, Scanlon, Davis, Gomez, and Brown [S3][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
No further action appears in the legislative record — the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the House never voted on the bill [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it; all bills not passed expire when a Congress ends [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Text-message marketers, telemarketers, and collection agencies are better off: the low-cost channel of automated texts to consumers remains open, since no competing law filled the gap before the Congress ended.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban automated unsolicited text messages and referred it to committee.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it six original supporters.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat without action from referral in July 2022 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would show broader support [S3][S4].

industries.note: Their business model depends on blasting automated texts to large lists of phone numbers; the bill makes unsolicited automated texts illegal without prior express consent, cutting off their cheapest outreach channel. Consumers gain the same consent protection for texts that telemarketing calls already have [S3].
The bill strikes the exception that let collectors autodial people over debts owed to or guaranteed by the United States without consent, so they would need to obtain consent or dial by hand [S3].

industries.industry: Businesses that send legitimate automated texts (appointments, delivery notices)
industries.note: Businesses that already obtain customer consent face little change, but they would bear the cost of consent records and reassigned-number database checks; in exchange, the safe harbor shields them from liability when a customer's number changes hands [S3].
